name: Brísingamen
powers: Heightens the beauty of its wearer; a treasure of the goddess Freyja.
description: The radiant necklace of the goddess Freyja, forged by the dwarves. In the Prose Edda it is counted among the treasures of the gods; in Lokasenna Loki accuses Freyja of having won it dishonorably from the dwarves. The hero Þórólfr and the god Heimdallr both fight over it in separate sagas, and Heimdallr retrieves it from Loki in the shape of a seal.

name: Bjargástafur
powers: Carries the bearer through danger and hardship unharmed.
description: Bjargástafur, the rescue stave of the Huld manuscript, drawn so that the bearer could escape or survive any danger. Its name derives from bjarga, 'to save', and the grimoire tradition promises that no misfortune could hold a person who bore it. It is one of the general talismans of protection in Icelandic folk magic.

name: Bridal Crown
powers: Marks the bride as a crowned bride, bringing honour to the wedding.
description: The bridal crown (brudkrona), a crown of gilt silver or brass that Swedish churches owned and lent to brides for the wedding ceremony. The custom, recorded from the Middle Ages, made the bride a 'crowned bride' and the crown a symbol of honour and virginity. Rules sometimes required a fee, and the crown was kept locked in the church between weddings.
source: Swedish church custom of the bridal crown

name: The Barrel Bung
powers: Conjures food, drink, or gold for its owner.
description: A barrel bung, the wooden stopper of a cask, that works magic in a Swedish folk tale. In the tale 'The Barrel Bung', the small wooden plug proves able to conjure food, drink, or gold for its owner. It is one of the many humble objects that Swedish wonder-tales turn into providers of plenty.

name: The Bewitched Knife
powers: Steel laid across the cradle keeps the changeling away; a knife breaks spells.
description: An iron knife that Swedish folk tradition used against harmful magic. A knife or other steel laid across a newborn's cradle was believed to keep the bortbyting, the changeling, from swapping the child, and a knife was also run through a bewitched churn or struck into the threshold to break spells. The sign-carved knife also served the healer in 'signing' rites.
source: Swedish folk belief in steel against harmful magic

name: The Broom King
maker: The broom itself in the tale
powers: Rules all brooms and sweeps away the story's dangers.
description: The broom king, the broom that rules all brooms, from the Swedish tale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'. In the tale a broom proves to be the king of its kind, sweeping away the story's dangers with a command that no other broom could match. The tale plays on the humble household object raised to kingship.
source: Swedish folktale 'The Broom's Broom King of All Brooms'

name: The Black Book of the Clergy
powers: Conjurations and signs for summoning and binding spirits.
description: The black book (svartbok), a manual of black magic that Swedish tradition placed in the hands of a priest or 'klok' man who had studied 'the black art'. Actual svartkonstböcker, filled with conjurations, signs, and instructions, survive in Swedish archives from the 17th-19th centuries; legend said the priest's black book could be passed on only on his deathbed.

name: Bukkehorn
description: A natural folk horn cut from a hollowed goat or cow horn and sounded through a mouthpiece pierced in the side. Herders used it on the summer seter pastures and at festive gatherings, carrying loud calls and dance tunes across mountain valleys. The horns range from small finger-hole instruments to long curved signal horns, and survived into the 20th century in Norwegian oral folk music.

name: Bunad
material: Wool and linen with silver brooches
description: The festive national costume of Norway, sewn from wool in patterns that vary by district, with embroidery, silver brooches, and distinct headwear. Modern bunads grew out of the folk dress of the 18th and 19th centuries and were revived and standardized in the 20th as a symbol of national identity. Hundreds of regional variants are worn at holidays, weddings, and Constitution Day.

name: Borgund Stave Church
description: The best-preserved of Norway's stave churches, built around 1180 in Borgund, Sogn. Its stacked tiers of steep roofs, dragon-head finials, and carved portals are the classic image of the stave church, and the interior keeps medieval altar furniture and runic graffiti. Because it was never drastically rebuilt, its timber frame and tarred shingles survive almost untouched.

name: Bridle of Bellerophon
maker: Brought by Athena in a dream
powers: Tamed the winged horse Pegasus so Bellerophon could ride it against the Chimera.
description: The golden bridle Athena gave Bellerophon to tame the winged horse Pegasus, allowing him to ride and, mounted, to defeat the fire-breathing Chimera; Apollodorus tells of the dream in which Athena brought the bridle, and Pausanias describes the shrine at Corinth where it was dedicated.
source: Apollodorus, Bibliotheca; Pausanias, Description of Greece

name: Cauldron of Rebirth
powers: Restored slain warriors to life, though the revived could not speak.
description: Pair Dadeni, the Cauldron of Rebirth in the Second Branch of the Mabinogi. Given to Brân the Blessed by a giant couple from Ireland, it restores slain warriors to life, though the revived cannot speak. In the war for Branwen the cauldron is finally shattered by Efnysien, who throws himself into it.

name: Briar Rose's Spinning Wheel
powers: Pricked the princess and cast the whole castle into a hundred-year sleep.
description: The spinning wheel in the Grimms' Dornröschen, whose spindle pricks the sleeping princess and sends the entire castle into a century of sleep. The king had ordered all spindles burned, but the old woman in the tower still spins. When the prince cuts through the thorns, the spindle's pricking is undone and the wheel stands still.

name: The Belt of Tahmineh
powers: Binds the bond between the lady of Samangan and the hero Rostam.
description: A belt said to be woven by Tahmineh of Samangan, mother of Sohrab, and given to the hero Rostam on the night of their meeting, binding their union in some tellings of the tale. The motif varies across recensions of the Shahnameh and in modern retellings, and Ferdowsi's text describes no single canonical belt, so the object's particulars rest on later tradition rather than the epic's own lines.

name: The Brazen Serpent
powers: Healed the Israelites bitten by desert serpents when they looked upon it.
description: The bronze serpent made by Moses at God's command to heal the Israelites bitten by serpents in the wilderness, raised on a pole so that the stricken who looked upon it lived. Kept in the Jerusalem Temple, it was later destroyed by King Hezekiah as an idol under the name Nehushtan. Its story is told in Numbers and 2 Kings, and the object itself is known only from scripture.

name: Bagua Mirror
powers: Deflects harmful energy (sha qi) and returns evil glances
description: A circular mirror ringed with the eight trigrams of the Book of Changes around a central yin-yang disc, hung over doorways in Chinese feng shui practice to turn away harmful energy (sha qi). Also paired with talismanic spells against hauntings, the bagua mirror is said to return an attacker's evil gaze and to guard the threshold from malign spirits.

name: Bangmangi
powers: Grants whatever the wielder wishes when struck
description: The magic club (bangmangi) of the Korean goblin dokkaebi, which in folktales grants whatever a person wishes when it strikes. Villagers trick the gullible dokkaebi into beating the club and losing it, or use it to draw endless food, gold, and healing; the club and its owner remain beloved fixtures of Korean storytelling.

name: Betel and Areca Tray
powers: Foundation of hospitality and marriage ritual
description: The tray that carries betel leaves, areca nut, and lime, the foundation of Vietnamese hospitality and marriage custom. In the founding legend, twin brothers Cao and Lang died for love of the same woman and became the areca tree and betel vine; chewing the combination remains a rite of respect, greeting, and kinship.
source: Betel and areca legend; folk custom

name: The Bayon Smile
powers: The king's watchful presence over the kingdom
description: The colossal stone face-towers of the Bayon temple at Angkor Thom, carved in the 12th century under Jayavarman VII with serene, downcast smiles. Khmer legend reads the many faces as the king's presence watching over the kingdom from every direction, and the towers remain the emblem of Angkor's guardian gaze.

name: Birchbark Canoe
material: Birchbark over cedar frame with spruce root lashing
powers: Glides silently over lakes and rivers, light enough to carry.
description: The light, silent canoe built of birchbark sewn over a cedar frame with spruce root, the great carrier of the Anishinaabe and other northern peoples across lakes and portages. A single canoe could be carried by one person and moved across hundreds of miles of waterways, which is why traders and explorers adopted it. Master builders still construct it with the same bark, gum and root joinery.
source: Anishinaabe oral tradition and historical accounts

name: Bolas
material: Balls of stone or iron joined by braided hide cords
era: From the colonial era to the present
powers: Entangles the legs of running cattle or game.
description: Two or three weights joined by braided cords, swung and hurled to wrap around the legs of fleeing cattle, horses or game, the signature hunting tool of the Argentine pampas and of the gaucho. The technique came to the region with the Indigenous peoples of the plains and was adopted wholesale by the colonial cattle herders. Versions were recorded among the Mapuche and other southern peoples.

name: Batá Drum
material: Carved hardwood with animal hide heads
era: Cuban Santería tradition to the present
powers: Talks the language of the orishas at ceremony.
description: The sacred twin drums of Cuban Santería, carved in an hourglass shape with heads of different sizes, played only by initiates in ceremonies where their rhythms are said to speak the language of the orishas. The drums descend from the Yoruba bata of West Africa, carried by enslaved people to Cuba and preserved behind Catholic saints. Each drum is consecrated and named when it is made.
source: Cuban Santería practice and music studies

name: Benin Bronze Plaque
maker: Igbesanmwan guild casters of the Igun quarter
description: Cast-brass wall plaques of the Edo Kingdom of Benin (in present-day Nigeria) once covered the Oba's palace pillars, depicting the king, warriors, and courtiers in high relief. Made by guild casters using lost-wax casting, they record royal history, protocol, and the kingdom's contact with Europeans. Taken to Europe in 1897, they remain central to restitution debate.
source: British Museum collections; Edo court history and restitution scholarship

name: Bogolanfini Mud Cloth
description: Bogolanfini, or mud cloth, is a Bamana textile of Mali painted with fermented river-mud dye over a yellow ground to create dark geometric patterns. Made by women, the cloth records proverbs and historical knowledge and was worn at initiations and by hunters; its designs are held to protect and to transmit clan memory.

name: Baule Goli Mask
description: The goli is a round-faced, carved mask of the Baule people of the Ivory Coast, painted and worn at village dances and funerals. Goli performances follow a fixed sequence of mask types that mirror the cosmos and communal order, and the mask is associated with the goli spirit forces that lend the dance its authority.

name: Bamum Beaded Throne (Mandu Yenu)
description: The Mandu Yenu is the beaded royal throne of the Bamum kingdom of Cameroon, a low platform completely covered with glass beads in layered patterns of royal symbolism. The 19th-century throne of King Nsangu is among the finest, framing the seated king with beaded figures and the two-faced mask of royal justice. Beaded thrones proclaimed the divine rank of the fon.
source: British Museum collections (Mandu Yenu of King Nsangu)

name: Bamileke Elephant Mask
era: Traditional, still used in chiefdom rites
description: Beaded wooden masks of the Bamileke of the Cameroon Grassfields, often shaped as an elephant head with rounded ears and trunk, are worn by the society that enforces chiefly authority. The elephant mask links the wearer to the fon's power and the forest, and beadwork in royal colours marks noble membership. Attribution to specific chiefdoms varies across museum collections.
source: Museum collections of Cameroon Grassfields royal arts

name: Buganda Royal Drum (Mujaguzo)
description: The mujaguzo are the royal drums of the Buganda kingdom of Uganda, a set of tuned drums beaten at coronations, the accession of chiefs, and war. The principal drum, also called Mujaguzo, is kept in the palace and beaten only on state occasions; the drums were regarded as the voice of the kabaka and his ancestors.

name: Burnous Cloak
description: The burnous is the hooded, sleeveless woollen cloak of the Berbers of North Africa, woven in one piece with a pointed hood (qob). Worn by men over other garments, it shields against sun and cold and marks status; finely embroidered burnouses are reserved for ceremonies and celebrations.

name: Brass Urli
description: Wide shallow brass bowl of South Indian households, filled with water and floating flowers or marigold blossoms and set in entrance courts and courtyards as a marker of hospitality and blessing. Urlis are also used as ritual lamps when oil-lit wicks are floated on the water, a practice seen at weddings and festival doorways across Kerala and Tamil Nadu.
source: South Indian household and wedding practice

name: Banarasi Sari
description: Handwoven silk sari of Varanasi, made with gold and silver zari thread in patterns of mangoes, flowers and mehrab arches that have been prized in Indian bridal wear for centuries. Weavers of the city have produced banarasi brocades since Mughal times, and the sari is treated as a family heirloom passed between generations of brides.

name: Butterfly Jigha
description: Jewel-studded turban ornament of Mughal court fashion, shaped as a butterfly with a spring that quivers as the wearer moves, pinned to the turban by nobles and princes. Mughal miniature painting shows such jigha ornaments at court, and surviving examples in museum collections are worked in gold with gemstones, worn in the regions that became Pakistan.
source: Museum holdings (e.g. V&A O73036) and Mughal painting

name: Bhutanese Festival Mask
description: Carved and painted wooden mask worn by dancers in the cham dances of Bhutanese monasteries, taking the faces of fierce deities, animals and the skeleton guardians of the faith. The masks appear at tsechu festivals held yearly at the dzongs, where the masked dances are believed to bless onlookers and drive away evil, and where each mask's design follows strict iconographic rules.
